cases.policy_row: Rust May: enumerated trait/inherent implementation candidates for dyn dispatch
cases.rationale: dispatch()'s g.greet() call is a dyn Greeter vtable call; English::greet and French::greet are both structurally viable targets regardless of which concrete type a given test actually passes at runtime (the graph has no per-call-site argument-flow analysis). Both tests are therefore May relative to the origin symbol 'greet' generically (the corpus scores the overload-set symbol, not one impl in isolation, since Rust allows multiple items sharing a trait method name).

cases.policy_row: Rust May: enumerated generic-bound dispatch candidates
cases.rationale: announce<S: Speaker> monomorphizes per call site, but the graph (built from unmonomorphized source) sees s.speak() as resolving to any Speaker implementor; Dog::speak and Cat::speak are both structurally viable. Genuinely May, distinct from the dyn case (static generic dispatch is knowable per-instantiation in principle, unlike a true vtable call), but this extractor makes no such distinction — both are recorded as trait-method dispatch May.

cases.policy_row: Rust May: enumerated trait/inherent implementation candidates for dyn dispatch
cases.rationale: render()'s d.describe() is a dyn dispatch call; the default trait method body and Gadget's override are both viable targets structurally. Neither test proves the other's variant is unreachable from the graph's point of view, so both are May, whether the concrete call uses the default body or an override.

cases.policy_row: Rust Unknown: unresolved function pointers/closures
cases.rationale: run(f) invokes an opaque fn() -> i32 value; the graph cannot bound the set of functions ever assigned to such a pointer without value-flow analysis this extractor does not perform. Per policy, an unresolved function pointer is Unknown, not May with one candidate (the candidate set itself is unproven, not just its cardinality).

cases.policy_row: Rust Unknown: unexpanded macros
cases.rationale: run()'s body is a macro invocation (call_target!()); the extractor does not expand declarative macros to see the target() call textually inside it, so this is Unknown by the policy's explicit 'unexpanded macros' clause, even though the expansion is a simple direct call.

cases.policy_row: Rust Must: proven direct/concrete dispatch with one viable target
cases.rationale: Meters(2) + Meters(3) resolves, at the concrete type Meters, to exactly one impl Add for Meters — genuinely unambiguous (Rust has no operator overload sets the way C++ does; a concrete type has at most one Add impl). True ground truth is Must. The current extractor flags every binary_expression in a Rust file as an unconditional coverage gap ('implicit-drop-or-operator-dispatch-not-certified'), so this is expected to score 'conservative' (actual Unknown), not 'unsound' — a real, measured extractor gap, not a corpus-authoring error.

cases.policy_row: Rust Unknown: unresolved function pointers/closures; a unique spelling match never qualifies as Must
cases.rationale: run's own parameter is named `target`, shadowing the top-level function; the call target() inside run's body calls the PARAMETER, not necessarily the top-level function (test_shadowed happens to pass the top-level target, but the graph must not assume that from the name alone). A same-named call inside a shadowing scope must not be certified Must from a bare name match.

cases.policy_row: Rust Must: proven direct/concrete dispatch with one viable target
cases.rationale: The call target(x) textually inside the closure |x| target(x) is an ordinary direct call syntactically (a call_expression whose function is the identifier 'target'); the closure being passed to .map() as a value does not make the CALL INSIDE its body dispatch-ambiguous -- only how the closure itself is invoked would be. This distinguishes 'call inside a closure' (should be Must, same as any other same-file direct call) from 'stored/invoked closure value' (fn-pointer-stored, Unknown).

cases.policy_row: Rust Unknown: unresolved function pointers/closures
cases.rationale: Runner::run invokes self.callback, a boxed trait-object closure value; the graph cannot bound which function(s) are ever boxed into a Runner.callback across the program without value-flow analysis. Distinct from call-inside-closure-body: here the closure/fn ITSELF is the thing being called indirectly, not a call textually inside a closure body.
